title: CHEMICAL AND PHYSICAL OBSERVATIONS IN GOLFO, DULCE, AN ANOXIC BASIN ON THE PACIFIC COAST OF COSTA RICA
summary: The founding hydrographic description of Golfo Dulce, based on two occupations of the basin eight days apart in March 1969. It established the basic template every later study works against: a ~200 m inner basin behind a ~60 m sill, oxygen falling to near zero below the pycnocline, nitrate consumed by denitrification below it, and only trace hydrogen sulfide near the bottom. Crucially, the two closely spaced surveys caught a renewal event in progress, which led Richards and colleagues to argue that the basin is flushed erratically rather than being permanently stagnant like Cariaco or Framvaren — the single most important structural fact about this water column.
verbatim_finding: Hydrographic data taken 8 days apart indicated an influx of ocean water into the basin. It appears from past observations in the eastern tropical Pacific that the basin erratically receives ocean water during winter and spring.
data_availability: No modern data deposit. Profile data (temperature, salinity, O2, NO3, NO2, NH4, PO4, SiO4, H2S) are published as tables and figures within the paper itself; the underlying 1969 cruise data are not online.
caveat: Two station occupations in a single month of one year. Everything about seasonality and interannual variation in this paper is inference, not observation.

title: Morphology and sediment structures in Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica
summary: Fourteen 18 kHz echosounder profiles run during the RV Victor Hensen expedition (January 1994), giving the first systematic map of the basin's shape and of the sediment structures on its floor. This is the physical geometry that controls the whole oxygen problem: it documents the ~60 m sill, the >200 m flat inner basin, and a steep NE-side tectonic fault scarp reaching ~170 m of relief. It also shows the flat inner basin is floored by turbidites delivered down channels, leaving most slope sediment undisturbed — relevant because turbidite deposition is later invoked to explain why sulfide does not accumulate.
verbatim_finding: is a fjord-like structure with a deep inner basin (>200 m) sheltered against the open Pacific by a shallow sill (60 m)
data_availability: Echosounder profile tracks and interpreted bathymetric map are reproduced as figures in the PDF. No digital soundings released; the raw 18 kHz records are not archived online.
caveat: Single-beam echosounder along 14 lines only — this is a reconnaissance, not a bathymetric survey. The journal's own DOI for this article does not resolve; cite by URL.

title: A biogeochemical survey of the anoxic basin Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica
summary: The RV Victor Hensen (January 1994) biogeochemical survey that re-occupied Richards' 1969 stations and turned Golfo Dulce into a working laboratory for anoxic-basin biogeochemistry. It quantifies respiration pathways through the water column and sediments, showing oxygen persisting to ~100 m, a pycnocline sitting above the 60 m sill, nitrate-rich water entering at sill depth, and denitrification at anoxic depths. Its key structural conclusion — that the reproduction of the 1969 zonation implies water exchange frequent enough to prevent strongly reducing conditions — is the basis for treating Golfo Dulce as a periodically flushed rather than permanently anoxic basin.
verbatim_finding: Nitrate-rich water entered the bay at sill depth, and denitrification was indicated at anoxic depths.
data_availability: Water-column chemistry, respiration rates, benthic flux measurements and sediment pore-water profiles are tabulated and plotted in the article. No separate data deposit.
caveat: One week of sampling (6–12 January 1994) in the dry season. The scanned PDF is OCR-degraded in places; check numeric values against the figures. The journal's DOI for this article does not resolve.

title: Microbiological observations in the anoxic basin Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica
summary: The microbiological companion to Thamdrup et al. (1996) from the same Victor Hensen cruise, combining Most-Probable-Number counts, microscopy and molecular techniques on the sulfur-cycling community. It supplies the mechanistic reason why the basin's sulfide stays low: sulfate-reducer numbers peak in and near the sediment rather than through the water column, and free-swimming sulfide oxidisers (Thiovulum, Thiospira) plus vacuolated Beggiatoa occupy the anoxic bottom water and sediment–water interface, consuming sulfide as it is produced.
verbatim_finding: Although no oxygen was present hydrogen sulfide was only detectable close to the sediment.
data_availability: MPN count tables and micrographs published in the article. No sequence accessions or data deposit (predates routine GenBank submission for this kind of survey).
caveat: Cultivation-based (MPN) counts strongly under-represent true abundance; superseded for community composition by later 16S sequencing work, though its sulfur-bacteria observations still stand.

title: Characterization of some Golfo Dulce drainage basin rivers (Costa Rica)
summary: The baseline survey of the freshwater end-member feeding Golfo Dulce: 15 sites below 100 m altitude across the Osa Peninsula and the Esquinas and Coto Colorado basins, sampled through 1996–1997 for basic physicochemistry and benthic invertebrates. It is the source most directly relevant to quantifying what the rivers actually deliver — dissolved oxygen stayed within a narrow well-oxygenated range at every site, while suspended solids varied enormously between and within rivers with discharge, which is the variable that governs the sediment and turbidity plumes entering the gulf.
verbatim_finding: The rivers that drain into Golfo Dulce, south Pacific coast of Costa Rica, are important since they serve as vehicles of transport of materials and nutrients towards the gulf
data_availability: Site-by-site physicochemical measurements and species lists are tabulated in the article. No discharge time series and no digital deposit.
caveat: Spot sampling over two years, not gauged discharge. Gives concentrations, not loads — it cannot be used directly to compute freshwater or nutrient flux into the gulf. Scanned PDF is OCR-degraded.

title: Sedimentation in a tropical fjord: Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica
summary: Surface sediments and 3.5 m cores used to work out where the material filling the basin comes from and how it is emplaced. The finding that matters for the water column is negative and important: the cores show no laminated sections, splitting instead into turbiditic basin deposits and undisturbed hemipelagic slope deposits. Persistent lamination is the classic signature of a permanently anoxic, unbioturbated basin floor; its absence here is independent sedimentological evidence that Golfo Dulce's bottom water is not continuously anoxic on geological timescales.
verbatim_finding: The large proportion of non-biogenic material (>90%) reflects the dominance of terrigenous sediment input to Golfo Dulce.
data_availability: Core logs, grain-size, organic carbon and carbonate data presented in figures within the paper. No public data deposit; the cores are held at Universität Bremen.
caveat: Springer paywall — abstract is public, full text is not. Worth requesting if core chronology matters.

title: N2 production by the anammox reaction in the anoxic water column of Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica
summary: The paper that made Golfo Dulce globally significant. Using 15N labelling in the anoxic water column, it showed that anaerobic ammonium oxidation — previously known mainly from sediments and engineered reactors — accounts for 19–35% of N2 production in a marine water column. Because Golfo Dulce's chemistry closely resembles that of open-ocean oxygen minimum zones, where a third to a half of global fixed-nitrogen removal occurs, this small Costa Rican basin became the proof of concept that anammox is a major term in the ocean nitrogen budget. Every subsequent OMZ nitrogen study cites it.
verbatim_finding: Here we show that this reaction is also important in the anoxic waters of Golfo Dulce, a 200-m-deep coastal bay in Costa Rica, where it accounts for 19-35% of the total N2 formation in the water column.
data_availability: Rate measurements and depth profiles presented in the figures; supplementary information on the Nature site. No raw data deposit.
caveat: Based on incubations from a limited number of casts. The 19–35% share is specific to Golfo Dulce at that time; anammox-vs-denitrification partitioning is known to vary strongly between and within OMZs.

title: Comportamiento de las masas de agua en el Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica durante El Niño (1997-1998)
summary: The only sustained time series of the Golfo Dulce water column: five stations visited monthly for two years spanning the strong 1997–1998 El Niño, with vertical profiles of temperature, salinity and dissolved oxygen. This is the source for seasonality and interannual variability — it separates inner-basin from outer-gulf hydrography and, most usefully, identifies twice-yearly intrusions of cold, saline, oxygen-rich Pacific water into the basin, tentatively linked to the same forcing that drives Gulf of Panama upwelling. That gives the renewal mechanism a periodicity and a regional driver rather than leaving it as 'erratic'.
verbatim_finding: Finally, biannual events in the influx of cold, high salinity, and oxygen rich oceanic water masses into the basin were detected.
data_availability: Monthly T/S/O2 profiles are shown as contoured sections and figures in the article. No digital deposit; underlying CTD/bottle data held at CIMAR-UCR.
caveat: Spanish text with English abstract. The two years sampled were dominated by an exceptionally strong ENSO event, so the 'normal' seasonal cycle is hard to separate from the anomaly. Journal DOI does not resolve.

title: A physical-oceanographic study of Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica
summary: The definitive physical oceanography of the gulf: field campaigns in 1999 and 2001 by CIMAR-UCR with the University of Bergen, combined with a three-dimensional numerical circulation model. It is the source for how the gulf actually moves water. Because Golfo Dulce sits near the equator, Coriolis is negligible, so cross-gulf structure is set by runoff, local wind and topography rather than rotation; along-gulf temperature and salinity gradients are maintained by the four inner rivers; and the vertical structure differs between the sill (three-layer flow) and the inner basin (two-layer estuarine circulation over near-stagnant deep water). Anyone modelling flushing of the anoxic layer starts here.
verbatim_finding: A three-layer current structure is dominating in the sill area while in the deeper inner part of the gulf a two-layer estuarine circulation takes place above slowly moving deep water.
data_availability: CTD sections, current-meter records and model output are presented as figures. Model setup (Blumberg–Mellor / POM-type) is described but neither the forcing files nor the model output are archived publicly.
caveat: Field data are from two campaigns; the model is not validated against a long current-meter time series. Journal DOI does not resolve — cite by URL.

title: Biogeochemical controls on the oxygen, nitrogen and sulfur distributions in the water column of Golfo Dulce: an anoxic basin on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica revisited
summary: The full synthesis of the 1994 water-column and sediment biogeochemistry, and the paper that puts numbers on the renewal question. It reports the deepest ~100 m as anoxic with sulfide below 7 µM and only transiently present, bacterial maxima where oxygen falls below 1 µM around 100 m, and a sub-pycnocline dissolved inorganic nitrogen deficit of 2.9 mol m-2. Combined with a salt-balance residence time of 35 ± 57 days it yields a DIN loss of 51 ± 85 mmol m-2 d-1. It also explains the two reasons sulfide never builds up: frequent oxygenated Pacific inflows in the water column, and scavenging by iron-rich turbidites in the sediment, the most recent emplaced between 1989 and 1992 on 210Pb dating.
verbatim_finding: Sulfide in the water column was maintained at low concentrations by frequent inputs of oxygenated water from the Pacific Ocean.
data_availability: Chemical profiles, respiration rates, bacterial counts and 210Pb sediment chronology are tabulated and plotted in the article. No separate data deposit; a copy is also held in the University of Southern Denmark research portal.
caveat: The residence-time estimate (35 ± 57 d) has an uncertainty larger than the estimate itself, so the derived DIN-loss rate should be treated as order-of-magnitude. Journal DOI does not resolve.

title: A snapshot view of some vertical distributions of water parameters at a deep (200 m) station in the fjord-like Golfo Dulce, embayment, Costa Rica
summary: Eight field trips between June 1993 and September 1995 profiling temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen and inorganic nutrients at 10 m intervals down the 200 m station. Its value is as a counterweight to the 'permanently anoxic' shorthand: across this whole period deep oxygen was low (3.00–0.20 mg/L) but never actually anoxic. It also resolves the physical structure — thermocline between 25 and 60 m, halocline near 40 m, a 34-salinity layer over a thick 35-salinity bottom layer — and attributes the nutrient-rich bottom water to sporadic ocean inflow over the 60 m sill. The vertical nitrite structure led the authors to infer anammox independently.
verbatim_finding: from 60 m depth down to the bottom (200 m), dissolved oxygen concentrations were low during the whole study, ranging from 3.00 mg/L to 0.20 mg/L, although anoxic conditions were not detected.
data_availability: Profiles for each of the eight cruises are given as figures and tables in the article. Underlying Niskin-bottle data held at CIMAR-UCR; not deposited.
caveat: Single station, eight occupations — explicitly a 'snapshot'. Its non-detection of anoxia over 1993–1995 sits in tension with contemporaneous reports of anoxia and H2S, which is itself the point: the deep layer is variable.

title: Caracterización físico-química de dos estuarios en la bahía de Golfito, Golfo Dulce, Pacífico de Costa Rica
summary: Eleven monthly cruises through 1998 across 12 stations in two mangrove estuaries of Golfito Bay, measuring salinity, temperature, dissolved oxygen, Secchi depth, suspended matter, dissolved inorganic nutrients and chlorophyll a. It characterises the small-scale, land-facing end of the gulf's hydrography: these estuaries are vertically well mixed rather than stratified, and they carry very high silicate (up to ~980 µmol/L in the rainy season) and strongly seasonal nitrate, with river-station concentrations far exceeding those in the mangrove channel and marine stations. This is the best quantification of the nutrient signal the eastern shore delivers to the gulf, and of its dry/rainy-season contrast.
verbatim_finding: Salinity profiles showed these are vertically mixed or well mixed estuaries, with no anoxic conditions
data_availability: Station-by-station monthly values for all measured variables are tabulated in the article, with dry/rainy season ranges given explicitly. No digital deposit.
caveat: Covers Golfito Bay only — not the Esquinas, Rincón or Coto Colorado inputs, which dominate the gulf's freshwater budget. Spanish text with English abstract; journal DOI does not resolve.

title: A carbonate platform associated with shallow cold methane seeps in Golfo Dulce, Pacific Costa Rica
container: Galaxea, Journal of Coral Reef Studies
summary: First report of a cold methane seep in shallow, warm, oxygen-saturated tropical water — a combination previously unknown outside hydrothermal settings. At 10 m depth the authors found a ~100 m2 carbonate platform standing ~2 m above mud, venting odourless high-methane gas, with pore water inside the platform at 5 µM O2 down to below detection while the overlying column was 97–100% saturated. Carbon isotope signatures of the crust point to authigenic carbonate formed by anaerobic oxidation of methane. It establishes that Golfo Dulce's methane story is not confined to the deep anoxic basin: there is a shallow geological methane source too.
verbatim_finding: For shallow tropical waters, methane seeps are only known from hydrothermal vents (Nakamura et al. 2006). Here, we report about our recent discovery of a cold methane seep in warm
data_availability: Photogallery-format note. Gas composition, O2 microsensor readings and stable carbon isotope values are reported in the text; underwater photographs are the primary figures. No data deposit.
caveat: A short 'Photogallery' contribution, not a full research paper — findings are described as preliminary by the authors. Superseded in detail by Salas et al. (2023).

title: Determination of Respiration Rates in Water with Sub-Micromolar Oxygen Concentrations
summary: A methods paper that matters for interpreting every oxygen-consumption number reported from Golfo Dulce. Using water from the Golfo Dulce anoxic basin alongside Chile–Peru OMZ water and nanomolar-sensitivity optode measurements, it shows that laboratory incubation artefacts inflate measured O2 consumption rates by 3 to 60 times as incubations are prolonged, with the inflation starting after 4–5 h in surface water and 10–15 h below the mixed layer, and that deoxygenation by gas bubbling and stirring further distort rates. It is the reason older long-incubation respiration estimates for low-oxygen waters should be treated as upper bounds.
verbatim_finding: we have explored how experimental conditions affect measured rates of O2 consumption in low-O2 waters from the anoxic basin of Golfo Dulce (Costa Rica) and oceanic waters off Chile-Peru
data_availability: Incubation time series and derived rates presented in figures. Open access under Frontiers CC-BY; no separate data repository deposit.
caveat: Methodological rather than descriptive — it uses Golfo Dulce water as material, and reports no new hydrography for the gulf.

title: Rasgos oceanográficos en el Golfo Dulce, Pacífico de Costa Rica: una revisión para la toma de decisiones en conservación marina
summary: A CIMAR review built on new sampling from September 2005 to November 2007 at five stations (GD1–GD5), assembling the physical, chemical, biological and meteorological picture of the gulf specifically for conservation decision-making. It reports the circulation as classic fjord-type estuarine, with surface currents near 18 cm/s at the gulf entrance falling to ~5 cm/s in the wide northwestern interior near Rincón, dominant east-west surface flow, ~5.4 cm/s southward flow off Puerto Jiménez, and near-bottom speeds of only 2.0–4.8 cm/s. Notably, over this period it did not find complete oxygen depletion between 70 and 140 m — a further data point that the deep layer's oxygen state varies between years.
verbatim_finding: El patrón de circulación de las aguas en el Golfo Dulce es el típico de estuarios tipo fiordo, con una estratificación de flujo en la columna de agua.
data_availability: Current velocities, hydrographic profiles, nutrient and zooplankton data from the 2005–2007 campaigns are presented in tables and figures. Open access (diamond) via Revista de Biología Tropical; no separate dataset deposit.
caveat: Five stations visited five times (GD5 only once) — thin coverage for the strong claims about circulation. Its non-detection of deep anoxia conflicts with other years and should not be generalised.

title: Hidrografía y plumas estuarinas en Golfo Dulce, Pacífico Sur de Costa Rica
summary: CTD profiling at 33 stations across the gulf in 2009–2010, aimed specifically at mapping the estuarine plumes from the rivers. This is the best quantitative treatment of freshwater influence: in August 2009 the plume between the Coto Colorado and Esquinas rivers depressed salinity below 30 over roughly 250 km2, about 37% of the gulf's surface, generating thermohaline fronts along almost the whole gulf. It characterises Golfo Dulce surface water as salinity <31.5 and temperature >27 °C occupying the top five metres, and captures the January 2010 El Niño peak as a contrasting state.
verbatim_finding: En agosto 2009, entre los ríos Coto Colorado y Esquinas disminuyeron la salinidad (<30) en un área de 250km2 aproximadamente, un 37% de la superficie total, creándose frentes termohalinos a lo largo de casi todo el golfo.
data_availability: CTD-derived salinity, temperature, sigma-T and current sections plus surface Secchi and chlorophyll-a values are mapped and tabulated in the article. Open access; underlying CTD casts not deposited.
caveat: Two survey periods only (Aug 2009, Jan 2010), one of them under strong El Niño conditions. Plume extent is therefore illustrative of two states, not a climatology.

title: Fixed-Nitrogen Loss Associated with Sinking Zooplankton Carcasses in a Coastal Oxygen Minimum Zone (Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica)
summary: Extends the Golfo Dulce nitrogen story from the free-living water column to particles. Using 15N enrichment on carcasses of abundant copepods and ostracods across the gulf's steep O2 gradient, it shows that sinking carcasses act as anoxic microbial hotspots hosting intense anaerobic nitrogen cycling even where ambient oxygen is present. Carcass-associated activity is dominated by DNRA, then denitrification, anammox and N2O production, whereas free-living bacteria in the anoxic bottom water run mainly anammox and denitrification. It reframes pelagic N-loss as partly a particle-scale phenomenon and identifies a route by which zooplankton indirectly fuel free-living anammox via ammonium release.
verbatim_finding: Carcass-associated anaerobic N-cycling was clearly dominated by dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) at up to 30.8 nmol NH4+ individual-1 d-1, followed by denitrification
data_availability: Rate data and water-column context (thermocline ~30–50 m; oxic / hypoxic-anoxic / anoxic layering across 0–40, 40–70, 70–100 m) given in figures and supplementary material on the Frontiers site. Open access CC-BY.
caveat: Per-individual rates from incubated carcasses; scaling them to a whole-water-column N-loss term depends on carcass abundance and sinking-speed assumptions that carry large uncertainty.

title: Evaluación preliminar del área agrícola y su influencia sobre la calidad del agua en el Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica
summary: Quantifies what the catchment delivers to the gulf besides water. Satellite-image mapping of the Esquinas, Coto Colorado, Rincón, Conte, Agujas, Tigre and Palma sub-basins found roughly 10 000 ha of rice and 31 000 ha of oil palm, with estimated annual application of 20.4 kg/ha of pesticide in rice, 6.6 kg/ha in oil palm and 840 kg/ha/yr of granulated fertiliser. Targeted sampling detected the herbicide clomazone in every water sample, plus triazophos, isoprothiolane and propiconazole in the Coto Colorado. It establishes the Coto Colorado as the overwhelmingly dominant agricultural drainage into the gulf, which matters both for nutrient loading and for contaminant delivery to the stratified basin.
verbatim_finding: en la subcuenca Coto Colorado, la cual abarca el 95 % del total del área agrícola que drena al golfo
data_availability: Cultivated-area estimates by sub-basin, pesticide/fertiliser use estimates from producer surveys, and residue concentrations in water, sediment and fish are tabulated in the article. Open access via Universidad Nacional; no separate deposit.
caveat: Explicitly preliminary: agrochemical use is estimated from secondary sources and surveys, not measured, and residue sampling was a single point-in-time exercise. Gives no fluxes.

title: A fjord-like tropical ecosystem, Pacific coast of Costa Rica: overview of research in Golfo Dulce
summary: The best single entry point to the Golfo Dulce literature: a synthesis of 123 studies, organised around the RV Victor Hensen expedition (1993–1994) and its follow-on microbiology, water-parameter studies, vertebrate work and zooplankton research, with the vertical oxygen and temperature profile literature discussed in detail. Its summary judgement is the most defensible one-line characterisation of the water column available — low oxygen below 50 m, frequent but not permanent anoxia in the 200 m basin, with occasional H2S formation. Useful for reconciling the apparently contradictory anoxia reports across the 1969–2020 record.
verbatim_finding: Golfo Dulce has low oxygen concentrations below 50 m and is frequently anoxic at the 200 m deep basin with occasional formation of H2S.
data_availability: Review; no new data. Its value as a resource is the compiled bibliography of 123 Golfo Dulce studies and its comparison of published oxygen/temperature profiles across decades. Open access (diamond).
caveat: Secondary source — use it to navigate to primaries, not as evidence in itself. Coverage of grey literature and theses is incomplete.

title: Anaerobic methane oxidation in a coastal oxygen minimum zone: spatial and temporal dynamics
summary: The strongest modern evidence on both the stability of the redox structure and the methane budget. Three consecutive years of sampling (2018, 2019, 2020) combining biogeochemistry, incubations and 16S rRNA sequencing show a redox zonation that is stable across years, with methane up to 1.7 µmol/L in anoxic bottom waters, yet high anaerobic methane oxidation in the OMZ core (rate constant averaging ~30 /yr in 2018 and ~8 /yr in 2019–2020). OPU3 and Deep Sea-1 Methylococcales clades peak 5–25 m below the oxic–anoxic interface and in the deep anoxic water respectively, implying a microbial filter that suppresses methane escape to the atmosphere.
verbatim_finding: Our results demonstrate a stable redox zonation across the years with high concentrations of methane
data_availability: Full data archive on Zenodo (CC-BY) with methane/nutrient concentrations, oxidation rates, kinetics and reference sequences; 16S amplicon data deposited in sequence archives as stated in the paper.
caveat: Wiley paywall on the article, though the underlying data are open. The three sampling years are all January–February, so seasonal (rainy-season) dynamics are not covered.

title: Data archive for Anaerobic methane oxidation in a coastal oxygen minimum zone: spatial and temporal dynamics
summary: The most valuable machine-readable dataset currently available for the Golfo Dulce water column: CSV files of methane, nitrite, nitrate and ammonium concentrations, anaerobic methane oxidation rates and rate kinetics, plus reference sequence files, from annual campaigns in January–February 2018, 2019 and 2020. Released CC-BY, it is directly usable for plotting depth profiles of the anoxic layer's nitrogen and methane chemistry without needing the paywalled paper. Version 2 corrects a calculation error in v1 that had underestimated in-situ methane concentrations to roughly a third of their true values.
verbatim_finding: Data collected during annual sampling campaigns to the coastal oxygen minimum zone of Golfo Dulce, carried out in January-February 2018, 2019 and 2020.
data_availability: Open CC-BY download of nutrient_and_methane_concentrations.csv, methane_oxidation_rates.csv, kinetics_of_anaerobic_methane_oxidation.csv, methylococcales.fa and methanofastidiosa.fa via Zenodo and its REST API.
caveat: Registered with a DataCite DOI (10.5281/zenodo.6377988), which is not in Crossref, so it is recorded here by URL. Use version 2 or later — version 1 methane concentrations are wrong by a factor of about three.

title: Shallow gas seeps in the Golfo Dulce, South Pacific of Costa Rica: geological, physicochemical, and biological characterization
summary: The systematic follow-up to Wild et al. (2015) on Golfo Dulce's shallow methane seepage, combining gas composition, water nutrient chemistry, rock petrology, fish and benthic cover censuses and cryptofauna sampling. It quantifies the emissions at 49.5% methane and identifies the host rock as sandstone of the Charco Azul Group, tying the seepage to the regional geology rather than to hydrothermal activity. Ecologically it records 18 fish species and 93 cryptofauna taxa, with a community structure unlike anything else on the Costa Rican Pacific coast, and reports Biffarius ghost shrimp new to the Eastern Tropical Pacific.
verbatim_finding: The seeps are composed of 49.5% methane and the rock that makes up the platform is sandstone from the Charco Azul Group.
data_availability: Gas composition, nutrient concentrations, benthic cover percentages and taxon lists reported within the preprint. Freely readable on Research Square; no separate data deposit found.
caveat: Preprint, version 1 — not peer-reviewed as retrieved. A Spanish-language version of the same work circulates as Moya (2023) via UCR. Check for a journal version before citing numbers.

title: Conociendo lo invisible de un fiordo tropical: estructura del bacterioplancton en el Golfo Dulce, Costa Rica.
container: ISMEL 2025 — Simposio de Microbiología (Universidad Nacional de Costa Rica)
summary: The first molecular characterisation of the Golfo Dulce bacterioplankton, from a cooperative oceanographic campaign between Costa Rican public institutions, private industry and NASA. Seven stations were sampled from coastal waters out to the most oceanic point of the gulf; 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (Illumina MiSeq) was paired with environmental (temperature, salinity) and inorganic-nutrient measurements. The reported result is a strong correlation between bacterioplankton distribution and the physicochemical variables, with Cyanobacteria, Rhodobacterales and some Bacteroidetes shifting in composition along the coast-to-ocean transect — the microbial community structure that older cultivation-based work (Kuever et al. 1996) could not resolve.
verbatim_finding: En el mundo existen únicamente cuatro fiordos tropicales, y el Golfo Dulce, ubicado en el Pacífico sur de Costa Rica, es uno de ellos.
data_availability: Conference abstract only; no sequence accessions, station coordinates or environmental data released with it. Contact carolina.marin.vindas@una.cr (Universidad Nacional, Escuela de Ciencias Biológicas) for the underlying data.
caveat: Conference abstract, not a peer-reviewed paper — roughly 300 words with no figures, tables or methods detail beyond the platform used. Treat all findings as provisional pending full publication.

title: Riparian vegetation reduces coastal turbidity
summary: Uses 33 years of remote sensing (1987–2019) over southern Costa Rica, including Golfo Dulce, with four causal-inference methods to quantify how catchment land use propagates into the gulf's water column as turbidity. It finds that a 15 m riparian natural-vegetation buffer significantly reduces gulf turbidity out to 800 m offshore, while pasture and gravel roads increase it, and that effects are strongest for short, steep or low-discharge rivers. Watershed-scale land-use composition, by contrast, showed no significant effect. This is the only source giving a multi-decadal, spatially explicit account of the terrestrial control on Golfo Dulce's surface optical properties.
verbatim_finding: We found that riparian natural vegetation (15 m buffer) significantly reduced gulf turbidity up to 800 m offshore, which overlaps with coral reefs and seagrass habitats.
data_availability: Open access (Nature Portfolio). Built on public Landsat archives and land-cover products; the paper's data and code availability statements point to the derived turbidity and land-use datasets.
caveat: Satellite-derived turbidity is a surface optical proxy, not a measured suspended-sediment load, and says nothing about the deeper water column or the anoxic layer.
